reviewAudit.timestampNote: The previous review timestamp lay in the future at audit time. reviewedAtUtc now denotes metadata reconciliation, not the historical live execution time.
reviewAudit.scope: Clarified synchronous application ingestion and the recorded readiness procedure. Preserved all smoke verdicts and counts; no new live smoke was run.

scopeNote: A separate live run on its own Chroma collection (the policy plus llm_context_document.pdf) and its own lifecycle document. The evaluation runner deliberately does not perform these checks, because they need several documents and lifecycle calls. It records answerStatus per case, never a blended finalStatus, consistent with evaluation/objective-review-schema.json's axis separation.
comparisonNote: The noisy-corpus questions use the same corpus, generator and retrieval configuration as the main run's core-contract cases, but on a different, contaminated collection (policy plus a genuinely off-topic PDF). Its answerStatus values are therefore comparable in kind to evaluation/runs/20260903T193000Z-objective-review.json, but its PASS/FAIL counts must not be summed into that run's totals.

configuration.generatorOverrideNote: The application was started with no AZURE_OPEN_AI_DEPLOYMENT_NAME and no deployment-name argument. Its startup log reported 'Resolved generator deployment=gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07', so these smokes exercise the configured default.

readinessMethod.note: The controller calls document ingestion synchronously before returning. This smoke checks stored chunks and additionally waits on the search path it evaluates; its recorded create step needed one search attempt. These observations do not independently establish a general claim about Chroma's internal atomicity.
readinessMethod.ingestion: poll Chroma until the expected chunk count for the document is present
readinessMethod.createSearchability: poll /doc-qa/chat until the question returns at least one source; this run needed one attempt
readinessMethod.replacement: poll until none of the v1 chunk ids remain - the chunk id is a hash of the chunk text, so a count alone cannot distinguish 'replaced' from 'not started'
readinessMethod.deletion: poll Chroma until zero chunks remain for the document name

noisyCorpus.rationale: POST /doc-qa/documents returned 202 after ingesting EPAM_JavaSecureCodingGD.md and llm_context_document.pdf into a fresh collection. A direct Chroma query confirmed 41 policy chunks and 33 PDF chunks before any question was asked, matching the 41-chunk policy manifest exactly.

verdicts.rationale: Names all three examples (cryptographic keys, passwords, algorithm) and both reasons (hostile JVMs can quickly view the data; obfuscation does not hide the code from serious attackers), exactly as section 2.1.6 states them. All five returned sources are policy chunks: the distractor PDF did not displace the policy.

Combines all three named sections with both ordering constraints preserved - validation after defensive copying (2.3.1), normalization before validation (2.3.4), sanitization before logging with the log-injection and cross-trust-boundary consequences (2.3.5) - and adds the policy's own caveat that blacklisting alone is insufficient.

Exactly five bullets, each grounded in a different policy passage and about a different theme, with no preface or conclusion. No bullet states who owns, approves, reviews or publishes the document, and no bullet is grounded in the distractor PDF: the distinctness and governance rules hold under corpus contamination.

A question about long-context language-model input and output length limits is answered entirely from llm_context_document.pdf; all five returned sources are PDF chunks and no policy chunk leaked into the answer. Retrieval discriminates between the two co-ingested documents in both directions.
The out-of-corpus Kubernetes question returns the exact refusal string with an empty source array, despite the larger and noisier corpus offering more plausible-looking material to over-retrieve.

lifecycle.createV1Rationale: After ingesting v1, the chat answer states the v1 content - do not hardcode API keys in configuration files committed to source control, because anyone with repository read access could recover the secret - and cites five sources. It also adds the policy's own 2.1.6 guidance, which is grounded in the co-ingested corpus, not invented.
lifecycle.replaceV2Rationale: After PUT-replacing with v2, none of v1's chunk ids remain in the collection, and the chat answer is exactly the v2 content: rotate API keys automatically on a fixed schedule and store them only in a managed secret vault. No stale v1 content leaked into the answer.
lifecycle.postDeleteRefusalRationale: The follow-up chat call after DELETE returned the exact refusal string with an empty source array.
lifecycle.manifestAbsenceRationale: A direct Chroma query after deletion returned 74 chunks split exactly 41 EPAM_JavaSecureCodingGD.md / 33 llm_context_document.pdf, with zero chunks under documentName secure-notes.md.
